newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: African countries urge foreign mining investment.
newsitem.headline: African countries urge foreign mining investment.

text.p: Several agriculture-dependent African countries on Thursday urged foreign mining companies to explore and invest in their mineral resources, a move which was seen loosening their reliance on farm products for growth.
Speakers at the Investing in African Mining Conference said the region held vast mineral reserves including gold, copper and platinum group metals.
But these resources had remained largely unexploited for reasons ranging from remoteness of terrain, structure of mineral rights' ownership and political instability, speakers said.

Swaziland's Simon Maphanga, senior geologist at the country's Surveys and Mines Department, told Reuters mining accounted for less than 10 percent of the kingdom's Gross Domestic Product with sugar, forestry, citrus and pulp activities contributing far more.
However, a number of foreign firms, notably South African mining house JCI Ltd and Canada's Southern Era had recently begun exploring for gold in the country, he said.

The head of Eritrea's department of mines, Alem Kibreab, said although 30 years of civil war had stunted the industry -- it had only ever had one operational copper and gold mine -- this was likely to change in the future.

"Agriculture is our mainstay at the moment but fisheries, light industry and minerals are expected to become our mainstay in the near future," Kibreab said, adding that seven international firms were currently exploring for minerals there.

Records of Japanese exploration in the 1970s at the Debarwa mine, now under licence to Australia's Western Minerals Corp Ltd, showed it held proven and probable ore reserves of around 800,000 tonnes at 2.5 percent copper and two g/t of gold.
It was estimated to hold a further 1.8 million tonnes at three percent copper and one g/t of gold. "The true size of the deposit is likely to be greatly in excess of this estimate," Kibreab said.

He said Eritrea had mapped out a number of incentives to lure investment ranging from duty-free export of minerals to overseas foreign currency accounts and full repatriation of earnings with no witholding taxes.
Malawi had also drawn up investor-friendly policies including import duty exemptions on capital equipment and zero tax for certain strategic projects, the country's delegation said.

They said several international companies including Caledonia Mining Corp and Consolidated Diamond Corp Ltd were involved in exploration, helping to lift mining's contribution to Malawi's GDP to over 10 percent in 1993 from only one percent in 1990.
